newsitem.title: USA: Viacom loses $217 million, hurt by Blockbuster charge.
newsitem.headline: Viacom loses $217 million, hurt by Blockbuster charge.

text.p: Entertainment giant Viacom Inc. said on Tuesday it lost $217 million in the second quarter, hamstrung by a $323 million pretax charge in its money-losing Blockbuster video rental business.

Excluding the Blockbuster charge, the loss was about $14 million, compared with a profit of $26 million a year ago. Viacom's revenues in the latest quarter rose to $3.03 billion from $2.79 billion, paced by double-digit growth in its MTV cable networks, Paramount movie business and Spelling Entertainment unit.
The loss, equal to 66 cents a share including the Blockbuster charge, or 8 cents without the charge, compared with a profit of 3 cents a share a year ago.
In addition to Blockbuster, Viacom owns film studio Paramount Pictures, music video channel MTV Networks, pay-cable channel Showtime Networks and book publisher Simon & Schuster.
Viacom said the $323 million charge resulted from store closings and overbuying of videotapes at Blockbuster. An expanded retail product mix also hurt margins at the video chain.
"In the second quarter, all of Viacom's business segments, aside from Blockbuster, turned in solid performances," said Sumner Redstone, chairman and chief executive.
He said the company has "to a large extent identified the issues which contributed to its unsatisfactory (Blockbuster) performance."

New management "is putting operational and marketing initiatives in place" to refocus the business, Redstone added. "We are optimistic that Blockbuster will enter a period of renewed growth next year."
Analysts said the company's ailing video business could still manage a recovery in the second half of this year.
"It's too early to tell, but indications are somewhat positive," said David Doft, an analyst at Furman Selz.
Analysts said Blockbuster's performance may be helped in the second half of the year by the release on video of a string of movies that did well at the box office.
In addition, comparisons with last year should improve because 1996 video rentals dropped while viewers watched the summer Olympics in Atlanta.

Analysts said it was still too early to judge the performance of John Antioco, who was named to run Blockbuster in June. They also noted that Viacom's other divisions performed well, especially networks and broadcasting.
"The quarter came in slightly better than my pessimistic expectations," said Jill Krutick, an analyst at Smith Barney. "Every business did slightly better out of the block.
New York-based Viacom reported second-quarter EBITDA -- or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization -- of $127 million, far below the $472 million a year ago.

For the quarter, cash flow at its entertainment businesses, including Paramount Pictures, decreased 17 percent to $95 million due to a change in Paramount's television product mix and lower profits from feature films. Revenues rose 14 percent to $862.3 million.

Networks and broadcasting revenues increased 11 percent to $626 million, while cash flow rose 19 percent to $200 million. Income from increased advertising sales and affiliate fees boosted cash flow at MTV by 15 percent, to $127 million.

Showtime networks' cash flow soared 63 percent, due in part to growth in the direct broadcast satellite industry in the United States. Showtime subscribers increased by nearly two million from a year ago to 17.1 million as of June 30.

Publishing revenues, including Simon & Shuster, edged up 4 percent to $535 million, while cash flow rose 6 percent to $56 million, helped by strong international sales in European, Asian and Latin-American markets.
Viacom's stock gained 25 cents to $30.44 in midafternoon trading on the American Stock Exchange.
